description: Comprehensive guide to identifying and valuing silver coins at estate sales

us_silver_coins.pre_1965_rule: All US dimes, quarters, and half dollars minted before 1965 are 90% silver (except 1942-1945 half dollars which are 40% silver for war nickels). Pennies are never silver.

dime.description: Smallest silver coin. Look for Mercury/Denis, Roosevelt, and Barber designs
dime.value_note: Even small, a bag of 100 dimes = 7.23 troy oz silver (~$180-200 melt value)

quarter.description: Look for Washington, Barber, and Seated Liberty designs
quarter.value_note: Bag of 40 quarters = 6.4 troy oz silver

half_dollar.value_note: Bag of 20 half dollars = 7.23 troy oz silver

morgan_dollar.description: Liberty head with eagle. Most collectible US silver dollar
morgan_dollar.value_note: $20-$1,000+ depending on date, mint mark, and condition

peace_dollar.description: Liberty head facing forward with eagle on reverse

identification_tips: Look for mint marks (small letters near date): D, S, O, CC, W
Edge should be reeded (grooved), not smooth
Weight and diameter should match specifications

crown.description: British crown = 5 shillings. Pre-1920 usually 92.5% silver

mexican.note: Common at US estate sales. Look for '868' or '900' marks

australian.description: Australian silver crowns and half crowns

chinese.note: Often found in estate sales with Asian heritage

coin_value_factors: Mint mark (S = San Francisco, D = Denver, CC = Carson City, O = New Orleans)
estate_sale_coin_tips: Check any jar of mixed coins for pre-1965 dimes/quarters
Look for coin albums and collections
Morgan dollars are the most collectible — check dates
British crowns and half-crowns often overlooked
Canadian 80% silver dollars (pre-1967) are easy to miss
Bag rolls of silver coins are often sold as 'copper' or 'mixed coins'
